segments.segment_summary:
Verdict: the belief is partly right and partly wrong, based on sources checked on 28 Sep 2026.

WRONG: "only 3D printer boards that are not industrial." Several PC-free controllers with screens are clearly CNC products, not printer boards. They have optically isolated 24 V-class I/O, differential step/dir, gantry slaving and ATC/probing logic.
- DDCS Expert (Digital Dream) has the same basic architecture as the planned product: ARM + FPGA pulse generator on Linux. It gives 1 MHz per axis, 24 isolated inputs and 21 isolated outputs, a 7-inch display and parameter backup/restore. Amazon reseller price is $430.
- DDCS V4.1 is $334-389 at the same reseller.
- Both DDCS units already sit inside or near the USD 249-400 target band, with a screen.
- MASSO G3 Touch (15-inch touch, 24 isolated inputs) is the benchmark for a finished commercial product, but it costs US$890-2,090 on the official store and core features are locked by software tier.

RIGHT: nothing I found combines this product's key features:
- **Motor channels:** Every PC-free product in this segment tops out at 5 step channels (MASSO 5, DDCS Expert 5, Redline/RealTime 5 drivers for 4 axes, Buildbotics 4). The only 6-8 axis options (Centroid AcornSix/Hickory) need a Windows PC and cost $999-1,999.
- **Axis encoders:** None of the PC-free products accepts axis encoders at the controller. MASSO's encoder input (60 kHz) is for the spindle only and its docs say servo encoders go to the drive. Redline and MASSO use drive alarm/error inputs instead.
- **Open design with a screen:** The only truly open standalone controller is Buildbotics (GPL software, CERN-OHL-S PCB, documented REST/WebSocket API and YAML config schema, config backup/restore). But it has 4 motors, 5 V I/O, no bundled screen and costs $499. Sienci says the SLB-EXT will be open-sourced later; it needs a $795 Windows touch PC.
- **Closed or tiered:** MASSO, DDCS, RealTime/Redline and Centroid are closed firmware. MASSO charges for Lua scripting ($2,090 tier) and for 5-axis/slaving/closed-loop ($1,090 tier).
- **Repair and CAD setup:** No product states repair by module without rewiring, a removable settings cartridge, or CAD-guided visual setup.
- **Packaged LinuxCNC:** I found no packaged, generally sold LinuxCNC + FPGA controller with an included touchscreen. LinuxCNC forum posts show DIY Pi 5 + Mesa + touchscreen builds, and a bare Mesa 7i96S is about EUR 239 with no screen.

Implications for the product:
1. The closest price and architecture competitor is DDCS, not a printer board. The product must beat it on channel count (8-12 vs 3-5), axis encoders, openness/CLI/API and repairability, at a similar price.
2. The "open, API-configurable" claim is not unique. Buildbotics already publishes an API and config schema, so the real difference is open + industrial 24 V + 8-12 channels + screen together.
3. "Industrial" claims in this segment are mostly marketing. None of the vendors checked cite IEC 61131-2 or similar I/O compliance, so this product could lead by publishing measured I/O ratings.

Could not verify:
- DDCS official manufacturer pricing. ddcnc.com has an expired TLS certificate and loads a script from an unrelated domain, so I used distributor-hosted manuals and Amazon reseller listings.
- Standalone price of the RealTime motion controller (only sold in bundles).
- Encoder inputs on DDCS and Buildbotics.
- Centroid CNC12 Pro/Ultimate license prices.
- Step rate of the Sienci SLB-EXT.

Also noted but not tabulated: Spark Concepts CNC xPRO V5 ($219, out of stock; 4 TMC5160 drivers, GRBL32/FluidNC web UI, 5/24 V selectable limits, no screen). It fits the "printer-style board" description, and its rate and I/O isolation are unverified.

segments.segment_summary:
Verdict on the user's belief ("nothing out there like this, only 3D-printer boards that are not industrial"): the belief is wrong as stated, but partly right about the specific combination.

1) The "only 3D-printer boards" part is wrong. Many controllers with a built-in screen, 24 V isolated I/O and no PC are sold for production machines. The closest match on price and architecture is the Digital Dream DDCS Expert (M350). It is built on FPGA pulse generation plus an ARM running Linux, drives 5 axes at 1 MHz with gantry slave support, has 24 isolated inputs and 21 outputs and a 7-inch screen, and runs on 24 VDC. Marketplace prices are roughly US$390-650 (reported, not published by the maker). That is inside or just above the planned US$249-400 band. It is closed firmware, has a key panel rather than a proper touchscreen, and is limited to 5 axes.

2) The lower-cost Asian industrial controls are real production products: GSK 980MDi, Weihong NK280/NK300CX PLUS, Syntec 6MA/6MB/60W-E, KND K1000MCi/K2000 and LNC M6800. They have 8-15 inch displays, 32-48 inputs by 16-38 outputs at 24 V (expandable to 72-128 points), PLC ladder, backup/restore, and one-key servo tuning (Weihong) or Auto-Servo Tuning (Siemens). Reseller and marketplace prices run about US$1,500-5,000 per controller, often with the maker's own bus servo drives. None publishes an MSRP. Most top out at 3-6 axes; the NK300CX PLUS reaches 10. They are sold mainly to machine builders (OEMs), not end users.

3) The Western entry-level controls cost much more. A Siemens 808D Advanced panel unit alone is US$5,167 at a US distributor (8.4 in, 4 axes plus spindle, 24 in/16 out). An 828D kit is about US$19.5k (reported). CNC1's do-it-yourself FANUC 0i-F Plus retrofit kits cost US$54,900-65,000 for 2-4 axes with drives and motors. Fanuc and Siemens support many axes (0i-MF Plus: 12 axes in one path, 14 in two) and touch displays, but they are closed, OEM-configured systems.

4) Tormach PathPilot is the one LinuxCNC-based industrial product. It is a GPL fork of LinuxCNC; source is by written offer, according to the LinuxCNC forum. It only runs Tormach machines officially. The controller computer is US$919.05 with no screen. A 17-inch resistive touch kit adds US$589. The Operator Console with a 17-inch touchscreen is US$2,529 (published on tormach.com). It is not sold as a general retrofit controller, and it has no step/dir or I/O board of its own for other machines (it relies on the machine's ECM).

What I found no product offering (from the sources checked; not proof that none exists): all of the following in one unit —
- at least 8 native step/dir motor channels, expandable to 12
- open, editable hardware and firmware
- CLI or AI-scriptable configuration with preview/diff
- repair by swapping modules plus a settings cartridge
- CAD-guided setup
- an included touchscreen
- US$249-400.

Each item exists somewhere on its own. The combination does not show up in this segment. The realistic competitive threat at the target price is DDCS-class Chinese standalone controllers, which already sell production-grade isolated 24 V I/O and a screen for about US$400-650. The pitch should be "open, 8-12 channels, touch, scriptable, modular", not "first industrial standalone controller with a screen".

Evidence limits:
- Most Asian prices are reseller or marketplace figures, not the maker's MSRP.
- KND and LNC specs came from search summaries and third-party pages; their official pages returned 404 or 403.
- Fanuc and Siemens do not publish list prices; the figures used are distributor or integrator prices.
- AliExpress and Alibaba product pages could not be fetched (login redirect or empty). Figures from them are search-snippet only.
- Currency conversions (HUF, ZAR) are approximate at unverified 2026 exchange rates.

segments.segment_summary:
Test of the claim that only 3D-printer boards exist and nothing industrial does. For this segment of PC-based controllers used with separate software, the evidence says the claim is false as stated. The more exact version is that nobody sells this as one packaged product at this price.

(1) Industrial-grade PC-based boards are common and have been the standard for years. The Mesa 7I96S (US$149), 7I95T (US$249), 7I76EU (US$219) and 7I97T (US$279) are FPGA Ethernet cards with isolated field I/O from 5-36 V and 36 V/2 A outputs. The 7I96S and 7I95T are rated to 10 MHz step rates. Mesa publishes the HostMot2 FPGA source (GPL and other licences) and the cards run LinuxCNC, including on a Raspberry Pi 5. Centroid's Acorn, AcornSix, Oak and Hickory add a proprietary but polished CNC12 stack. AcornSix lists a configuration wizard, automatic firmware and driver installs, config backup and restore, auto-squaring of paired axes, and optional expansion to 9 encoders.

(2) Cheap controllers with 8 or more channels already exist, but they are not industrial. PoKeys57CNC has 8 axes at 125 kHz for EUR119 ex VAT (US$162.85 at CNC4PC). PlanetCNC Mk3 has 9 axes at 110 kHz for EUR175 plus a EUR69 licence, ex VAT. Both have limited isolated I/O.

(3) No product in this segment includes a touchscreen or compute. Every one needs a separate PC or Pi, a screen, usually a breakout board and power supplies, and often a paid licence. Centroid says a 1920x1080 display is required and recommends a touchscreen.

(4) What a complete touchscreen system really costs, with estimates marked. The cheapest industrial-grade route is DIY: Raspberry Pi 5 4GB (about US$110 after the 2026 memory price increases) + official 10-inch Touch Display 2 (US$80) + Mesa 7I96S (US$149) + supplies/SD/case. That comes to about US$385-420 but gives only 5 step/dir channels, 1 encoder and 11 inputs / 6 outputs, with no enclosure. Swapping in the 7I95T gives 6 step/dir channels and 6 encoders for about US$500-520. Commercial Windows-based systems work out to about US$600-950 for CNCdrive UC400ETH or ESS/Mach4, about US$750-1,200 for Acorn with a Pro licence, and US$1,600-2,000+ for AcornSix, Oak or Hickory. Centroid's own CNC PCs cost US$899-1,350.

(5) Where the gap really is: this price range with an included touchscreen, 8 motor channels expandable to 12, 4 encoders, isolated 24 V I/O, open hardware and firmware, CLI/AI-scriptable configuration and repair by module. Centroid comes closest on guided setup and backup, but it is closed and costs 3-5x more. Mesa plus a Pi comes closest on architecture and price, but it is a parts kit with fewer channels. Mesa board schematics are not published, which I did not verify further.

Threats to watch: the PlanetCNC Mk4 has been announced but I did not verify it is shipping (reported as Ethernet, 8 axes, about 50 inputs / 50 outputs, no EtherCAT). Pi 5 + Mesa images are officially supported: LinuxCNC 2.9.8 Pi 4/5 image, 21 January 2026; current release 2.9.10. Mesa Configuration Tool II already gives a GUI setup wizard for 7I96S, 7I95T, 7I76EU and 7I97T.

Unverified: I could not reach the CNCdrive main shop page because of a PHP error, but individual product pages worked. USD figures converted from EUR are approximate. Generic Windows mini-PC and touchscreen monitor prices are my own estimates, not from primary sources.

segments.segment_summary:
Verdict: the user's belief is partly true and needs a narrower wording. As of 28 Sep 2026 I found no product in this segment that combines all of the following: at least 8 differential STEP/DIR channels with per-channel enable and alarm, 4 encoder inputs, protected and isolated 24 V I/O, local LinuxCNC on a compute module, an included 7-21 inch touchscreen, and modular repair. It is not true that the segment is "only 3D-printer boards that are not industrial". Several products already cover individual parts of the concept:

(1) Architecture and price. BTT Manta M8P V2.0 + CB2 + HDMI7 (US$268.74 + $72.58 = about $341 at biqu.equipment today) already sells compute module + 8 motor channels + 7-inch touch screen inside the proposed price window. It is printer-grade: StepStick sockets, 5 V-clamped endstops, no isolation, no differential outputs, no encoders, and Klipper is not a full CNC interpreter.

(2) Industrial features from printer-derived firms. Duet 3 MB6XD ($242.99, Filastruder):
- 6 external-driver ports with fault inputs
- 4 opto-isolated I/O pairs rated 12-50 V
- CAN-FD expansion, including 1XD differential single-axis boards and 1HCL closed-loop encoder boards ($105.99)
- RepRapFirmware CNC mode with G54 work offsets
- open schematic/BOM
- 7-inch DuetScreen ($122.99)
Its step outputs are single-ended 5 V (20 mA). The 1XD's measured step rates are 30-83 kHz. RRF is not LinuxCNC. The per-axis CAN boards push the cost of a full 8-channel machine well above $400.

(3) Industrial-leaning open boards:
- Expatria Flexi-HAL ($108 USD, CERN-OHL-S): isolated differential step/dir, differential spindle encoder, LinuxCNC through Remora and a Pi. Only 5 axes, no screen.
- Sienci SLB-EXT ($240): 5 differential step outputs with alarm, enclosed, E-stop. No screen, no encoders.
- PiBot V5.88 Ultra ($69.99): 10 opto-isolated inputs, isolated RS485.
- Mesa 7i96S ($149; open HostMot2 firmware, closed hardware): the reference. 11 isolated inputs, 6 isolated outputs, 10 MHz step. Only 5 axes.

(4) The closest open FPGA/LinuxCNC match to the planned endpoint is LiteX-CNC on Colorlight 5A-75B/5A-75E. It is GPL-3.0 with an open toolchain, generates steps on the FPGA at about 400 kHz, reads encoders and connects over Ethernet or SPI. It is a hobby firmware project on repurposed LED-receiver cards, with no industrial I/O or product support.

Industrial vs printer-grade ranking in this segment:
- Closer to industrial: Duet 6XD with 1XD/1HCL, Flexi-HAL, SLB-EXT, then PiBot V5.88 for input isolation only.
- Printer-grade: BTT Octopus Pro/Max EZ and Manta (5 V buffered step, 5 V-clamped inputs, no isolation), plus FluidNC 6x/6-Pack and T41U5XBB (5 V single-ended step, isolated inputs only).
- Remora turns BTT SKR/Octopus-class boards (and Flexi-HAL, EC500/NVEM) into LinuxCNC I/O endpoints, but the electrical interface stays printer-grade.
- Klipper-for-CNC is a set of community forks with basic CNC coverage (missing items include work coordinate systems, some canned cycles and helical moves). It is not a credible industrial path.

No product here offers a settings cartridge, repair-by-module without rewiring, CAD-guided setup, or a CLI/AI setup that keeps UI and CLI on one contract. The closest are FluidNC/PiBot (YAML plus browser WebUI, no compile), Remora-RT1052 (TFTP config upload) and LiteX-CNC (JSON board config). Those are the real differentiators.

Main competitive risk: a buyer can assemble "Flexi-HAL or Mesa 7i96S + Pi + 7-inch screen", or "Manta M8P + CB2 + HDMI7", for about $250-350 today. The product must win on:
- 8-12 differential channels
- 4 encoders
- isolated 24 V I/O
- the integrated, qualified package
Price alone will not do it.

Unverified items:
- whether LinuxCNC/Remora runs on the H723-based Manta/Octopus Max EZ (Remora lists only F4/LPC variants)
- Colorlight board retail prices (marketplace only)
- step rates for BTT, FluidNC and PiBot boards
- the 1XD price
- the T41U5XBB output buffering type
